chapter_text:
CHAPTER 23 — LIFE PROCESSES - 2: CONTROL AND COORDINATION

Introduction

A living organism is not a loose collection of independent organs. Its many parts work together in a precise, well-timed manner so that the body behaves as a single coordinated whole. When you touch a hot object you instantly pull your hand away; when you run, your heart beats faster and your breathing deepens; a plant bends towards light over hours and days. All of these are examples of CONTROL AND COORDINATION — the processes by which the activities of different organs are regulated and harmonised so that the organism responds appropriately to changes in its surroundings. A change in the environment that an organism detects and responds to is called a STIMULUS, and the change in the organism is called a RESPONSE.

23.1 THE NEED FOR CONTROL AND COORDINATION

Organisms must constantly detect changes (stimuli) such as light, heat, sound, touch, chemicals and gravity, and must respond to them quickly and correctly to survive. Different organs must act in the right sequence and at the right intensity — for example, during digestion the stomach, pancreas, liver and intestine must secrete their juices in proper order. Maintaining a steady internal environment (homeostasis), reproducing at the right time, and growing in an orderly way all demand coordination. In ANIMALS this control is achieved by TWO systems working together: the NERVOUS SYSTEM (fast, electrical, short-lived effects carried by nerves) and the ENDOCRINE SYSTEM (slower, chemical, longer-lasting effects carried by hormones in the blood). In PLANTS, which have no nervous system, coordination is achieved entirely by chemical messengers called plant hormones, producing slow movements.

23.2 THE NEURON — STRUCTURAL AND FUNCTIONAL UNIT OF THE NERVOUS SYSTEM

The nervous system is made of specialised cells called NEURONS (nerve cells). A neuron is the longest type of cell in the body and is specialised to receive, conduct and transmit information in the form of electrical impulses. A typical neuron has three parts:
 - CELL BODY (cyton): contains the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm; it carries out the cell's metabolic activities and processes incoming signals.
 - DENDRITES: short, branched projections arising from the cell body that RECEIVE information (stimuli) and carry impulses TOWARDS the cell body.
 - AXON: a single, long fibre that carries the impulse AWAY from the cell body towards the next cell. The axon may be covered by an insulating fatty MYELIN SHEATH which speeds up conduction. The axon ends in fine branches with knob-like nerve endings.

NERVE IMPULSE AND THE SYNAPSE
Information travels along a neuron as an electrical signal called a NERVE IMPULSE. When a stimulus is received by the dendrite, it sets off a chemical-electrical change that travels down the dendrite, through the cell body and along the axon to its endings. The tiny gap between the nerve ending of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron (or a muscle/gland) is called a SYNAPSE. The electrical impulse cannot jump the gap directly; instead it triggers the release of chemicals called NEUROTRANSMITTERS, which cross the synapse and start a new electrical impulse in the next neuron. Thus the synapse ensures the impulse travels in ONE direction only. Where a neuron meets a muscle, the junction is called a neuromuscular junction.

23.3 THE HUMAN NERVOUS SYSTEM

The human nervous system is divided into two main parts:
 - CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS): the BRAIN and the SPINAL CORD. It receives information, processes it, and issues commands.
 - PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (PNS): all the nerves that branch out from the brain (cranial nerves) and the spinal cord (spinal nerves) and connect the CNS to every part of the body.
Nerves are of three functional types: SENSORY (afferent) nerves carry impulses from sense organs TO the CNS; MOTOR (efferent) nerves carry commands FROM the CNS to muscles and glands (effectors); and MIXED nerves contain both kinds of fibres.

THE BRAIN AND ITS PARTS
The brain is the master coordinating organ, protected by the skull (cranium) and by three membranes (meninges) with a cushioning cerebrospinal fluid. It has three major regions:
 - FOREBRAIN, dominated by the CEREBRUM — the largest, most folded part. It is the seat of intelligence, memory, reasoning, will, learning, emotions and consciousness, and it controls voluntary actions. It also receives and interprets sensations such as sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch.
 - MIDBRAIN and HINDBRAIN, which include:
    • CEREBELLUM — the second-largest part; it maintains POSTURE and BALANCE and coordinates precise voluntary muscular movements (for example, walking in a straight line or picking up a pencil).
    • MEDULLA OBLONGATA (part of the brain stem) — controls INVOLUNTARY actions such as heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, coughing, sneezing, swallowing and vomiting.
The BRAIN STEM connects the brain to the spinal cord and regulates basic life-sustaining functions.
The SPINAL CORD is a cylinder of nerve tissue running down the backbone (vertebral column); it conducts impulses to and from the brain and is the centre for reflex actions.

23.4 REFLEX ACTION AND THE REFLEX ARC

A REFLEX ACTION is a sudden, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus, in which the response is so quick that the brain is not consulted first. Examples include pulling the hand away from a hot object, blinking when an object approaches the eye, knee-jerk, sneezing and the watering of the mouth at the smell of food. The pathway taken by the impulse during a reflex action is called the REFLEX ARC. In a typical reflex arc:
 1. A RECEPTOR (e.g. heat receptors in the skin) detects the stimulus.
 2. A SENSORY NEURON carries the impulse to the SPINAL CORD.
 3. In the spinal cord, a connecting (relay/inter) neuron passes the impulse to a MOTOR NEURON.
 4. The MOTOR NEURON carries the command to an EFFECTOR (a muscle), which produces the RESPONSE (the hand is withdrawn).
Because the spinal cord handles the response directly, reflexes are extremely fast and protect the body from harm. The brain is informed afterwards, which is why we feel the pain a moment later.

23.5 THE ENDOCRINE SYSTEM — CHEMICAL COORDINATION

Alongside the nervous system, the body uses a slower chemical control system. ENDOCRINE GLANDS (ductless glands) secrete chemical messengers called HORMONES directly into the BLOOD, which carries them to distant TARGET ORGANS where they act in very small amounts. Hormones regulate growth, development, metabolism, reproduction and the body's response to stress. The major endocrine glands and their hormones are:
 - PITUITARY GLAND (at the base of the brain): the 'master gland'. It secretes GROWTH HORMONE (controls the growth of the body; too little causes dwarfism, too much causes gigantism) and also controls the activity of other endocrine glands.
 - THYROID GLAND (in the neck): secretes THYROXINE, which regulates the rate of metabolism (carbohydrate, fat and protein use). Thyroxine needs IODINE; a lack of iodine in the diet causes the deficiency disease GOITRE (swelling of the thyroid).
 - ADRENAL GLANDS (one above each kidney): secrete ADRENALINE, the 'fight-or-flight' or emergency hormone. It raises the heartbeat, breathing rate and blood pressure and diverts blood to the muscles, preparing the body to deal with danger, fear or excitement.
 - PANCREAS: a dual gland. Its endocrine part secretes INSULIN, which lowers blood glucose by helping cells take up sugar. A deficiency of insulin causes the disease DIABETES MELLITUS, in which blood-sugar level rises.
 - TESTES (in males): secrete TESTOSTERONE, which controls the development of male sex organs and male secondary sexual characters (deep voice, facial and body hair).
 - OVARIES (in females): secrete OESTROGEN (and progesterone), which control the development of female sex organs and female secondary sexual characters and regulate the menstrual cycle and pregnancy.

FEEDBACK CONTROL
The amount of each hormone is precisely regulated by FEEDBACK mechanisms. For example, when blood-sugar rises after a meal, the pancreas releases more insulin; as the sugar level falls, insulin secretion is reduced. Such feedback keeps hormone levels and body conditions within healthy limits.

23.6 DIFFERENCES BETWEEN NERVOUS AND HORMONAL CONTROL

Both systems coordinate body activities but differ in important ways. NERVOUS control: the message is an electrical impulse; it travels along nerves; it is very FAST; its effect is short-lived; and it acts on specific muscles or glands. HORMONAL (endocrine) control: the message is a chemical (hormone); it travels through the BLOOD; it is comparatively SLOW; its effect is widespread and longer-lasting; and it usually controls long-term processes such as growth and reproduction. The two systems often work together — for instance, the nervous system can trigger the adrenal glands to release adrenaline.

23.7 COORDINATION IN PLANTS

Plants have neither nerves nor muscles, yet they too respond to stimuli — through chemical coordination and slow movements. Plant movements are of two broad kinds: TROPIC (directional) movements and NASTIC (non-directional) movements.

TROPIC MOVEMENTS (TROPISMS)
A tropism is a growth movement of a plant part in response to a directional stimulus; the DIRECTION of the movement is determined by the direction of the stimulus. Growth towards the stimulus is positive; away from it is negative.
 - PHOTOTROPISM: response to LIGHT. Shoots grow towards light (positive); roots grow away (negative).
 - GEOTROPISM (gravitropism): response to GRAVITY. Roots grow downward, towards gravity (positive); shoots grow upward, away from gravity (negative).
 - HYDROTROPISM: response to WATER. Roots grow towards a source of moisture (positive).
 - CHEMOTROPISM: response to a CHEMICAL. For example, the growth of the pollen tube towards the ovule through the style is a chemotropic movement.
 - THIGMOTROPISM: response to TOUCH or contact. The tendrils of climbing plants coil around a support they touch.

NASTIC MOVEMENTS
These are non-directional movements in which the direction of the response does NOT depend on the direction of the stimulus, and they are usually faster than tropisms. The folding of the leaves of the sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica, the 'touch-me-not') when touched, and the opening and closing of flowers in response to light or temperature, are nastic movements. These are caused by sudden changes in the water content (turgor) of certain cells rather than by growth.

PLANT HORMONES (PHYTOHORMONES)
Coordination and growth in plants are controlled by chemical messengers called plant hormones, made in one part and acting in another:
 - AUXIN: produced at the shoot tip; promotes cell elongation and is responsible for phototropism and geotropism (it accumulates on the shaded/lower side and makes that side grow faster, bending the plant).
 - GIBBERELLINS: promote the growth of the stem, help seeds germinate and cause flowering and fruit growth.
 - CYTOKININS: promote CELL DIVISION; they are found in greatest amounts in rapidly dividing regions such as fruits and seeds, and they delay the ageing of leaves.
 - ABSCISIC ACID (ABA): a growth INHIBITOR; it inhibits growth, promotes the closing of stomata and causes the wilting and falling (abscission) of leaves; it is sometimes called the stress hormone.
 - ETHYLENE: a gaseous hormone that promotes the RIPENING of fruits.

SUMMARY

- Control and coordination keep the many parts of an organism working together as a single unit, allowing it to detect a stimulus and make a suitable response.
- In animals, coordination is shared by the fast, electrical NERVOUS SYSTEM and the slow, chemical ENDOCRINE SYSTEM.
- The NEURON (cell body, dendrites, axon) is the unit of the nervous system; impulses cross the gap between neurons — the SYNAPSE — with the help of neurotransmitters, ensuring one-way flow.
- The nervous system has a CENTRAL part (brain + spinal cord) and a PERIPHERAL part (nerves). The CEREBRUM controls thought and voluntary action, the CEREBELLUM controls balance and coordination, and the MEDULLA controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat and breathing.
- A REFLEX ACTION is a fast, automatic response; its pathway is the REFLEX ARC (receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector).
- Endocrine (ductless) glands secrete HORMONES into the blood: pituitary (growth hormone), thyroid (thyroxine), adrenal (adrenaline), pancreas (insulin), testes (testosterone) and ovaries (oestrogen).
- Plants coordinate through plant hormones (auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid, ethylene), showing tropic movements (phototropism, geotropism, hydrotropism, chemotropism, thigmotropism) and nastic movements.

chapter_summary.title: Life Processes - 2: Control and Coordination — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 23. It explains why organisms need control and coordination, describes coordination in animals through the nervous and endocrine systems (the neuron, the brain and spinal cord, reflex action, and the major hormones), and describes coordination in plants through tropic and nastic movements and plant hormones.

sections.heading: Need for control and coordination
bullets: Organisms must detect changes in their surroundings (stimuli) and react suitably (responses) to survive.
Different organs must act in the correct order and intensity, and the internal environment must be kept steady (homeostasis).
In animals two systems coordinate the body — the nervous system (fast, electrical) and the endocrine system (slow, chemical); plants use only chemical hormones.

sections.heading: The neuron and the nerve impulse
bullets: A neuron has a cell body (cyton) with the nucleus, branched dendrites that receive impulses, and a single long axon that carries the impulse away.
Information travels as an electrical NERVE IMPULSE from dendrite to cell body to axon endings.
The gap between two neurons is the SYNAPSE; the impulse crosses it as chemicals (neurotransmitters), which makes transmission one-way.

sections.heading: The human nervous system and the brain
bullets: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system is all the nerves connecting the CNS to the body.
The CEREBRUM is the seat of intelligence, memory, reasoning and voluntary action and interprets sensations.
The CEREBELLUM maintains posture, balance and the coordination of precise movements; the MEDULLA OBLONGATA controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat, breathing and swallowing.

sections.heading: Reflex action and the endocrine system
bullets: A reflex action is a sudden, automatic, involuntary response; its pathway (reflex arc) is receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector.
Because the spinal cord acts directly, reflexes are very fast and protect the body from harm.
Endocrine (ductless) glands pour hormones into the blood: pituitary (growth hormone), thyroid (thyroxine), adrenal (adrenaline), pancreas (insulin), testes (testosterone), ovaries (oestrogen).

sections.heading: Coordination in plants
bullets: Tropic movements are directional growth responses: phototropism (light), geotropism (gravity), hydrotropism (water), chemotropism (chemicals), thigmotropism (touch).
Nastic movements (e.g. the folding of Mimosa leaves) are non-directional and are caused by changes in turgor rather than growth.

Plant hormones coordinate growth: auxin (elongation, tropisms), gibberellins (stem growth, germination), cytokinins (cell division), abscisic acid (inhibits growth, closes stomata), ethylene (ripening).

key_takeaways: Control and coordination let an organism respond to a stimulus with a suitable response and keep its parts working as one unit.
In animals the fast electrical nervous system and the slow chemical endocrine system share the task of coordination; plants use only hormones.
The neuron (cell body, dendrites, axon) carries impulses, which cross synapses as neurotransmitters in one direction only.
The cerebrum controls thought and voluntary action, the cerebellum controls balance and coordination, and the medulla controls involuntary actions.
A reflex action follows the reflex arc through the spinal cord, making it fast and protective.
Major hormones: growth hormone (pituitary), thyroxine (thyroid; needs iodine), adrenaline (adrenal), insulin (pancreas), testosterone (testes), oestrogen (ovaries).
Plants show tropic and nastic movements coordinated by auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene.

glossary.definition: A change in the environment (such as light, heat, touch or a chemical) that an organism detects and responds to.
The change or reaction produced in an organism as a result of a stimulus.
A nerve cell — the structural and functional unit of the nervous system, specialised to receive and transmit nerve impulses; made of a cell body, dendrites and an axon.
A short, branched projection of a neuron that receives impulses and carries them towards the cell body.
The single long fibre of a neuron that carries the nerve impulse away from the cell body to the next cell.
The microscopic gap between the nerve ending of one neuron and the next cell, across which the impulse is carried by chemical neurotransmitters, ensuring one-way flow.
The brain and the spinal cord, which receive information, process it and issue commands.
The largest part of the brain; the seat of intelligence, memory, reasoning and voluntary action, and the centre that interprets sensations.
The part of the brain that maintains posture and balance and coordinates precise voluntary movements.
The part of the brain stem that controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing and vomiting.
A sudden, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus, controlled by the spinal cord, in which the brain is not consulted first.
The pathway taken by an impulse during a reflex: receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector.
A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland into the blood, which acts in small amounts on distant target organs.
A ductless gland that pours its hormone directly into the blood (e.g. pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas).
A directional growth movement of a plant part in response to an external stimulus such as light, gravity, water, chemicals or touch.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Control and Coordination (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-23 for Lesson 23. Attempt all questions. Draw labelled diagrams where asked.

questions.question: Define a stimulus and a response. Give one example of each from your own daily life.
questions.answer: A STIMULUS is a change in the environment that an organism detects and responds to — for example, the ringing of the school bell (sound) or touching a hot vessel (heat). A RESPONSE is the reaction produced by the organism as a result of the stimulus — for example, getting up to leave when the bell rings, or quickly pulling the hand away from the hot vessel. Stimulus and response together are the basis of control and coordination.
questions.explanation: Definition of stimulus and response with everyday examples.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of a neuron and name its three main parts. State the function of each part.
questions.answer:
A neuron diagram should show the CELL BODY (cyton) in the middle with the nucleus, several short branched DENDRITES arising from it, and one long AXON leading away (often shown with a myelin sheath and end branches).
 - Cell body (cyton): contains the nucleus; carries out the cell's metabolic activity and processes signals.
 - Dendrites: receive impulses and carry them towards the cell body.
 - Axon: carries the impulse away from the cell body to the next neuron, muscle or gland.
questions.explanation: Label cell body, dendrites and axon; give each function.

questions.question: What is a synapse? Explain how a nerve impulse crosses it and why this makes transmission one-way.
questions.answer: A SYNAPSE is the tiny gap between the nerve ending (axon terminal) of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron (or a muscle/gland). The electrical impulse cannot jump the gap directly. When it reaches the axon ending, it triggers the release of chemicals called NEUROTRANSMITTERS, which diffuse across the gap and start a new impulse in the next neuron. Because the transmitter is released only from the axon side and received only on the dendrite side, the impulse can travel in ONLY ONE direction.
questions.explanation: Synapse as a gap; neurotransmitter chemicals carry the signal across in one direction.

questions.question: Name the three major parts of the human brain and write one function of each.
questions.answer:
(1) CEREBRUM — the seat of intelligence, memory, reasoning, will and consciousness; it controls voluntary actions and interprets sensations (sight, hearing, touch, etc.).
(2) CEREBELLUM — maintains posture and balance and coordinates precise voluntary muscular movements.
(3) MEDULLA OBLONGATA — controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, coughing, sneezing, swallowing and vomiting.
questions.explanation: Cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla with their functions.

questions.question: What is a reflex action? Describe the reflex arc with the help of a suitable example, naming each component in order.
questions.answer:
A REFLEX ACTION is a sudden, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus, in which the response is produced so quickly that the brain is not consulted first. Example: pulling the hand away on touching a hot object.
The pathway followed by the impulse is the REFLEX ARC:
 1. RECEPTOR — heat receptors in the skin of the hand detect the hot stimulus.
 2. SENSORY (afferent) NEURON — carries the impulse from the receptor to the SPINAL CORD.
 3. SPINAL CORD — a relay (inter) neuron passes the impulse from the sensory neuron to the motor neuron; the spinal cord acts as the coordinating centre.
 4. MOTOR (efferent) NEURON — carries the command from the spinal cord to the effector.
 5. EFFECTOR (arm muscle) — contracts and withdraws the hand.
Because the response is organised at the level of the spinal cord rather than the brain, it is extremely fast and protects the body from injury; the brain is informed a moment later, which is when we feel the pain.
questions.explanation: Definition + the five components of the reflex arc in order, with the hot-object example.

questions.question: Name the gland that secretes (a) thyroxine, (b) insulin, (c) adrenaline, (d) growth hormone.
questions.answer:
(a) Thyroxine — THYROID gland.
(b) Insulin — PANCREAS (its endocrine part).
(c) Adrenaline — ADRENAL glands (above the kidneys).
(d) Growth hormone — PITUITARY gland (the master gland).
questions.explanation: Matching hormone to its endocrine gland.

questions.question: A person's diet lacks iodine. Which gland and which disease are likely to be affected? Explain briefly.
questions.answer: The THYROID gland is affected. Thyroxine, the hormone of the thyroid, contains IODINE, so a lack of iodine in the diet means the gland cannot make enough thyroxine. The thyroid enlarges (swells) in an attempt to compensate, producing the deficiency disease GOITRE — a visible swelling of the neck. Adequate iodine (for example, from iodised salt) prevents it.
questions.explanation: Iodine deficiency affects the thyroid and causes goitre.

questions.question: Compare nervous control and hormonal (endocrine) control of the body under the headings: nature of message, path of travel, speed, and duration of effect.
questions.answer:
NERVOUS CONTROL:
 - Nature of message: an electrical nerve impulse (with a chemical step at synapses).
 - Path of travel: along nerves (neurons) to specific muscles or glands.
 - Speed: very fast (almost instant).
 - Duration of effect: short-lived; stops as soon as the impulse stops.
HORMONAL (ENDOCRINE) CONTROL:
 - Nature of message: a chemical — a hormone.
 - Path of travel: carried by the BLOOD to distant target organs all over the body.
 - Speed: comparatively slow.
 - Duration of effect: longer-lasting and often widespread; controls long-term processes such as growth and reproduction.
The two systems often cooperate — for example, the nervous system can stimulate the adrenal gland to release adrenaline in an emergency.
questions.explanation: Four-point comparison of nervous vs hormonal control.

questions.question: Define tropism. Name and explain any three types of tropic movements in plants.
questions.answer:
A TROPISM is a directional growth movement of a plant part in response to an external stimulus, where the direction of the movement is decided by the direction of the stimulus.
Three types:
 - PHOTOTROPISM (response to light): shoots grow towards light (positive), helping leaves catch sunlight.
 - GEOTROPISM (response to gravity): roots grow downward towards gravity (positive) and shoots grow upward (negative).
 - HYDROTROPISM (response to water): roots grow towards a source of moisture in the soil.
questions.explanation: Definition + any three of photo-, geo-, hydro-, chemo-, thigmotropism.

questions.question: Match each plant hormone to its main role: auxin, gibberellin, cytokinin, abscisic acid, ethylene.
questions.answer:
AUXIN — promotes cell elongation at the shoot tip and is responsible for phototropism and geotropism (bending).
GIBBERELLIN — promotes growth of the stem, helps seeds germinate and aids flowering/fruit growth.
CYTOKININ — promotes cell division and delays the ageing of leaves.
ABSCISIC ACID (ABA) — a growth inhibitor; closes stomata and causes wilting and falling of leaves (stress hormone).
ETHYLENE — a gaseous hormone that promotes the ripening of fruits.
questions.explanation: Five plant hormones matched to their roles.

questions.question: Why do living organisms need control and coordination?
questions.answer: Organisms must constantly detect changes (stimuli) in their surroundings and respond suitably to survive. Their many organs must act in the right order and intensity, the internal environment must be kept steady (homeostasis), and growth and reproduction must be regulated. Control and coordination link all the parts so the body works as a single, well-organised unit.
questions.explanation: Need to detect stimuli, respond, keep organs working together and maintain homeostasis.

questions.question: Distinguish between a stimulus and a response with one example.
questions.answer: A STIMULUS is a change in the environment that an organism detects, e.g. a bright light shining into the eye. A RESPONSE is the reaction the organism produces, e.g. the pupil of the eye becoming smaller. The stimulus comes first and triggers the response.
questions.explanation: Stimulus = environmental change; response = the reaction.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a neuron.
questions.answer: A neuron has three parts: (1) the CELL BODY (cyton), which contains the nucleus and cytoplasm and carries out the cell's metabolism; (2) DENDRITES, short branched fibres that receive impulses and carry them towards the cell body; and (3) the AXON, a single long fibre that carries the impulse away from the cell body to the next cell. The axon may be covered by an insulating myelin sheath and ends in fine branches.
questions.explanation: Cell body, dendrites and axon with their roles.

questions.question: What is a synapse and what is its role?
questions.answer: A synapse is the tiny gap between the axon ending of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron (or a muscle or gland). Its role is to pass the nerve impulse from one neuron to the next using chemical neurotransmitters, and to ensure the impulse travels in one direction only.
questions.explanation: Gap between neurons; passes impulse one way via neurotransmitters.

questions.question: Trace the path of a nerve impulse within a single neuron.
questions.answer: A stimulus is received by the DENDRITES, which carry the impulse TO the CELL BODY (cyton). From the cell body the impulse passes into the AXON, which carries it AWAY to the axon endings, from where it is passed across the synapse to the next cell. The flow is therefore dendrite → cell body → axon.
questions.explanation: Dendrite to cell body to axon.

questions.question: Explain why a nerve impulse can travel across a synapse in only one direction.
questions.answer: At a synapse, the chemical neurotransmitter is stored and released only from the axon ending of the first neuron. The receiving membrane on the dendrite of the next neuron has the receptors that detect the transmitter. Because the transmitter is released on one side and received on the other, the signal can only pass from the axon side to the dendrite side — never the reverse. This one-way arrangement keeps information flowing in the correct direction through the nervous system.
questions.explanation: Transmitter released only from the axon side and received only by the dendrite side.

questions.question: Name the two main divisions of the human nervous system and what each contains.
questions.answer: (1) CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS) — the brain and the spinal cord; it processes information and issues commands. (2) PERIPHERAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (PNS) — all the nerves (cranial and spinal) that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.
questions.explanation: CNS (brain + spinal cord) and PNS (nerves).

questions.question: Distinguish between sensory, motor and mixed nerves.
questions.answer: SENSORY (afferent) nerves carry impulses FROM the sense organs and receptors TO the central nervous system. MOTOR (efferent) nerves carry commands FROM the central nervous system TO the effectors (muscles and glands). MIXED nerves contain both sensory and motor fibres and so can carry impulses in both directions.
questions.explanation: Sensory = to CNS; motor = from CNS; mixed = both.

questions.question: How are the brain and spinal cord protected?
questions.answer: The brain is enclosed in a bony case called the cranium (skull) and the spinal cord runs inside the vertebral column (backbone). In addition, both are wrapped in three protective membranes called the meninges, and a cerebrospinal fluid between the membranes cushions them against shocks.
questions.explanation: Bony cases (skull, backbone), meninges and cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.question: State the functions of the cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla oblongata.
questions.answer: CEREBRUM: the seat of intelligence, memory, reasoning, will and consciousness; controls voluntary actions and interprets sensations. CEREBELLUM: maintains posture and balance and coordinates precise voluntary movements. MEDULLA OBLONGATA: controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing and vomiting.
questions.explanation: Three brain parts and their main functions.

questions.question: A man involved in an accident loses control of his heartbeat and breathing. Which part of the brain is likely injured? Why?
questions.answer: The MEDULLA OBLONGATA is likely injured. The medulla controls involuntary vital actions such as heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure. Damage to it disturbs these automatic functions, which is why the heartbeat and breathing become uncontrolled.
questions.explanation: Medulla controls involuntary heartbeat and breathing.

questions.question: Why is the cerebellum important for an athlete or a dancer?
questions.answer: The cerebellum maintains posture and balance and coordinates precise, smooth voluntary movements. An athlete or dancer relies on accurate balance and finely coordinated muscle action; the cerebellum ensures these movements are smooth, well-timed and properly balanced, preventing clumsy or uncoordinated motion.
questions.explanation: Cerebellum controls balance and fine coordination.

questions.question: What is a reflex action? Give two examples.
questions.answer: A reflex action is a sudden, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus, in which the response occurs so quickly that the brain is not consulted first. Examples: pulling the hand away on touching a hot object, and blinking the eye when an object suddenly comes near it.
questions.explanation: Definition + two examples of reflexes.

questions.question: List, in order, the components of a reflex arc.
questions.answer: The components of a reflex arc, in order, are: (1) RECEPTOR — detects the stimulus; (2) SENSORY NEURON — carries the impulse to the spinal cord; (3) SPINAL CORD (with a relay/inter neuron) — passes the impulse to the motor neuron; (4) MOTOR NEURON — carries the command to the effector; (5) EFFECTOR (muscle or gland) — produces the response.
questions.explanation: Receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron, effector.

questions.question: Why are reflex actions faster than ordinary voluntary actions?
questions.answer: In a reflex action the impulse is processed directly at the level of the spinal cord through a short reflex arc, without first travelling up to the brain for a conscious decision. This shorter pathway means the response is produced almost instantly, which is why reflexes are faster than voluntary actions that involve thinking by the brain.
questions.explanation: Reflexes bypass the brain and act through the short spinal pathway.

questions.question: How do reflex actions help in protecting the body? Justify with an example.
questions.answer: Reflex actions protect the body by producing an immediate, automatic response to harmful stimuli, before the slower conscious brain can react. For example, when a hand touches a hot pan, the reflex arc through the spinal cord makes the arm muscle withdraw the hand at once, limiting the burn. Similarly, blinking protects the eye from dust or a fast-approaching object. Because no time is lost in conscious thought, the body avoids or reduces injury.
questions.explanation: Immediate automatic response avoids injury; example of hot object/blinking.

questions.question: What are hormones? How do they reach their target organs?
questions.answer: Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by endocrine (ductless) glands. They are poured directly into the BLOOD, which carries them all over the body to distant target organs, where they act in very small amounts to control processes such as growth, metabolism and reproduction.
questions.explanation: Chemical messengers carried by the blood to target organs.

questions.question: Name the hormone, the gland and one function for: growth hormone, thyroxine and adrenaline.
questions.answer: GROWTH HORMONE — secreted by the PITUITARY gland; controls the growth of the body (too little causes dwarfism, too much gigantism). THYROXINE — secreted by the THYROID gland; regulates the rate of metabolism (and needs iodine). ADRENALINE — secreted by the ADRENAL glands; the emergency 'fight-or-flight' hormone that raises heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure.
questions.explanation: Hormone-gland-function for three hormones.

questions.question: What is the role of insulin? What happens when it is deficient?
questions.answer: Insulin is a hormone secreted by the endocrine part of the PANCREAS. It lowers the level of glucose (sugar) in the blood by helping body cells take up and use sugar. When insulin is deficient, blood-sugar levels rise and remain high, causing the disease DIABETES MELLITUS.
questions.explanation: Insulin lowers blood sugar; its lack causes diabetes.

questions.question: Why is iodised salt recommended in the diet?
questions.answer: Iodine is needed by the thyroid gland to make the hormone thyroxine. If the diet lacks iodine, the thyroid cannot make enough thyroxine and enlarges, causing the deficiency disease goitre. Iodised salt supplies the small amount of iodine the body needs, preventing goitre and keeping thyroxine production normal.
questions.explanation: Iodine is needed for thyroxine; iodised salt prevents goitre.

questions.question: Name the hormones secreted by the testes and ovaries and state one function of each.
questions.answer: The TESTES secrete TESTOSTERONE, which controls the development of male sex organs and male secondary sexual characters (such as a deep voice and facial hair). The OVARIES secrete OESTROGEN, which controls the development of female sex organs and female secondary sexual characters and helps regulate the menstrual cycle.
questions.explanation: Testosterone (testes) and oestrogen (ovaries) with functions.

questions.question: Just before a race, a runner's heartbeat and breathing speed up even before the race begins. Explain the role of a hormone in this.
questions.answer: This is caused by the hormone ADRENALINE, secreted by the ADRENAL glands. In situations of excitement, fear or stress, adrenaline is released into the blood and prepares the body for vigorous action ('fight or flight'). It raises the heartbeat and breathing rate, increases blood pressure and diverts more blood to the muscles, so the runner's body is ready for the extra effort even before the race starts.
questions.explanation: Adrenaline (fight-or-flight) raises heartbeat and breathing in stress.

questions.question: Give three differences between nervous control and hormonal control.
questions.answer: (1) The message in nervous control is an electrical nerve impulse, while in hormonal control it is a chemical hormone. (2) Nervous messages travel along nerves, whereas hormones travel through the blood. (3) Nervous control is very fast and its effect is short-lived, while hormonal control is slower but its effect is longer-lasting and more widespread.
questions.explanation: Message type, path, and speed/duration differ.

questions.question: Why is hormonal control suitable for processes like growth and reproduction?
questions.answer: Growth and reproduction are slow, long-term processes that must continue steadily over weeks, months or years rather than for an instant. Hormones are released into the blood and produce slow, widespread and long-lasting effects, which is exactly what such gradual processes need. Fast, short-lived nervous signals would not be suitable for controlling them.
questions.explanation: Hormones give slow, long-lasting, widespread control suited to growth/reproduction.

questions.question: Both the nervous and endocrine systems coordinate the body. Why does the body need both instead of just one?
questions.answer: The two systems suit different needs. The nervous system gives fast, precise, short-lived responses to specific muscles or glands — ideal for quick reactions such as withdrawing a hand or focusing the eye. The endocrine system gives slower, widespread and longer-lasting control — ideal for sustained processes such as growth, metabolism and reproduction. Having both lets the body respond instantly to emergencies AND regulate long-term internal processes; the two systems also cooperate, for example when the nervous system triggers the release of adrenaline.
questions.explanation: Fast precise nervous control + slow lasting hormonal control together cover all needs.

questions.question: Distinguish between tropic and nastic movements in plants.
questions.answer: TROPIC movements are directional growth movements in which the direction of the response depends on the direction of the stimulus (for example, a shoot bending towards light). NASTIC movements are non-directional movements in which the direction of the response does NOT depend on the direction of the stimulus (for example, the folding of Mimosa leaves on touch) and are usually faster and due to changes in turgor rather than growth.
questions.explanation: Tropic = directional, growth-based; nastic = non-directional, turgor-based.

questions.question: Name and describe any three types of tropism.
questions.answer: PHOTOTROPISM — growth in response to light; shoots bend towards light (positive). GEOTROPISM — growth in response to gravity; roots grow downward (positive) and shoots grow upward (negative). THIGMOTROPISM — growth in response to touch; tendrils of climbers coil around a support they touch. (Hydrotropism — towards water; and chemotropism — towards a chemical — are also valid.)
questions.explanation: Any three of photo-, geo-, hydro-, chemo-, thigmotropism described.

questions.question: State one function each of auxin, cytokinin and abscisic acid.
questions.answer: AUXIN — promotes cell elongation at the shoot tip and brings about phototropism and geotropism (bending of the plant). CYTOKININ — promotes cell division and delays the ageing of leaves. ABSCISIC ACID — a growth inhibitor that closes the stomata and causes wilting and the falling (abscission) of leaves; it acts as a stress hormone.
questions.explanation: Auxin (elongation), cytokinin (cell division), ABA (inhibits growth).

questions.question: A gardener finds that raw fruits ripen faster when kept with already-ripe fruits. Which hormone explains this?
questions.answer: The hormone ETHYLENE explains this. Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone that promotes the ripening of fruits. Ripe fruits release ethylene gas, which speeds up the ripening of the nearby raw fruits, so keeping raw and ripe fruits together makes the raw ones ripen faster.
questions.explanation: Ethylene gas from ripe fruit promotes ripening of raw fruit.

questions.question: Explain how auxin causes a shoot to bend towards light.
questions.answer: Auxin is made at the tip of the shoot and promotes cell elongation. When light falls on one side of the shoot, auxin moves towards the SHADED (darker) side and collects there. The cells on the shaded side, having more auxin, elongate (grow) faster than the cells on the lit side. This unequal growth makes the shoot bend TOWARDS the light — the response we call positive phototropism.
questions.explanation: Auxin gathers on the shaded side; faster growth there bends the shoot towards light.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A neuron is specialised to receive and transmit information as nerve impulses. A stimulus is first picked up by short branched fibres, passed through the part containing the nucleus, and then carried along a single long fibre to the next cell across a small gap.

(i) Name the short branched fibres that receive the impulse.
(ii) Name the part containing the nucleus.
(iii) Name the single long fibre that carries the impulse away.
(iv) What is the small gap between two neurons called?
questions.answer:
(i) DENDRITES.
(ii) The CELL BODY (cyton).
(iii) The AXON.
(iv) The SYNAPSE.
questions.explanation: Identifies dendrite, cell body, axon and synapse from their roles.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

At the end of an axon, a nerve impulse reaches a tiny gap before the next neuron. The impulse cannot jump the gap as electricity; instead, certain chemicals are released that carry the message across.

(i) What is the gap called?
(ii) What are the chemicals that cross the gap called?
(iii) In which direction can the impulse cross the gap?
(iv) Why is this one-way crossing useful?
questions.answer:
(i) The SYNAPSE.
(ii) NEUROTRANSMITTERS.
(iii) In one direction only — from the axon side to the dendrite side of the next neuron.
(iv) It keeps information flowing in the correct direction through the nervous system, preventing signals from running backward and getting confused.
questions.explanation: Synapse, neurotransmitters, one-way flow and its usefulness.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The human brain has three major regions. One large folded region is the seat of thinking and memory; a second region just below and behind it keeps the body balanced; a third region at the base controls vital automatic activities.

(i) Name the large folded region and one of its functions.
(ii) Name the region that controls balance.
(iii) Name the region that controls heartbeat and breathing.
(iv) Which of these controls voluntary actions?
questions.answer:
(i) The CEREBRUM — it is the seat of intelligence, memory and reasoning (and interprets sensations).
(ii) The CEREBELLUM.
(iii) The MEDULLA OBLONGATA.
(iv) The CEREBRUM controls voluntary actions.
questions.explanation: Cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla identified by function.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

When Ravi accidentally touched a hot plate, he pulled his hand away at once, even before he felt the pain. A moment later he felt the heat.

(i) What kind of action is pulling the hand away?
(ii) Which part of the central nervous system controls this action?
(iii) Write the pathway (reflex arc) followed by the impulse.
(iv) Why did Ravi feel the pain only a moment later?
questions.answer:
(i) A REFLEX ACTION (sudden, automatic, involuntary).
(ii) The SPINAL CORD.
(iii) Receptor (skin) → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (arm muscle), which withdraws the hand.
(iv) The reflex through the spinal cord acted first and withdrew the hand; the impulse reached the brain slightly later, so the sensation of pain was felt only a moment afterwards.
questions.explanation: Reflex action, spinal cord control, reflex-arc pathway and timing of pain.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Reflex actions such as blinking, sneezing and withdrawing the hand happen without our conscious control. They are organised through the spinal cord rather than the thinking part of the brain.

(i) Define a reflex action.
(ii) Give two more examples of reflex actions.
(iii) Why are reflexes not controlled by the cerebrum?
(iv) How does this benefit the body?
questions.answer:
(i) A reflex action is a sudden, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus, occurring without conscious thought.
(ii) Examples: the knee-jerk response and the watering of the mouth at the smell of food (also: coughing, blinking).
(iii) Because routing the impulse to the cerebrum for a conscious decision would take longer; the spinal cord handles it directly so the response is much faster.
(iv) The faster response protects the body from harm — for example, the hand is withdrawn from danger before serious injury occurs.
questions.explanation: Definition, examples, why spinal not cerebral, and protective benefit.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Endocrine glands are ductless glands that pour chemical messengers directly into the blood. These messengers act in tiny amounts on distant organs to control body processes.

(i) What are these chemical messengers called?
(ii) Why are endocrine glands called ductless glands?
(iii) Name the gland called the 'master gland'.
(iv) Name the gland that secretes thyroxine.
questions.answer:
(i) HORMONES.
(ii) Because they have no ducts (tubes); they release their hormones directly into the blood rather than through a duct.
(iii) The PITUITARY gland.
(iv) The THYROID gland.
questions.explanation: Hormones, ductless glands, pituitary and thyroid.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Meena often felt very thirsty, passed a lot of urine, and a blood test showed a high sugar level. The doctor said a certain hormone was not being produced in sufficient amount by one of her glands.

(i) Which hormone is deficient?
(ii) Which gland produces this hormone?
(iii) Name the disease.
(iv) What is the normal role of this hormone?
questions.answer:
(i) INSULIN.
(ii) The PANCREAS (its endocrine part).
(iii) DIABETES MELLITUS.
(iv) Insulin normally lowers the level of glucose in the blood by helping the body's cells take up and use sugar; without enough of it, blood sugar stays high.
questions.explanation: Insulin deficiency from the pancreas causes diabetes; insulin lowers blood sugar.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The body is coordinated by two systems. In one, messages travel as electrical impulses along nerves and act within a fraction of a second. In the other, chemical messengers travel through the blood and their effects are slower but last longer.

(i) Name the two systems.
(ii) Which system gives faster responses?
(iii) Which system controls long-term processes such as growth?
(iv) Give one way the two systems work together.
questions.answer:
(i) The NERVOUS system and the ENDOCRINE (hormonal) system.
(ii) The nervous system gives faster responses.
(iii) The endocrine (hormonal) system controls long-term processes such as growth.
(iv) The nervous system can stimulate the adrenal gland to release adrenaline during an emergency, so the two systems act together.
questions.explanation: Nervous vs endocrine: speed, long-term control, and cooperation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A potted plant kept near a window was seen to bend its shoot towards the light over a few days, while its roots grew downward into the soil. These are directional growth responses controlled by plant hormones.

(i) What is the bending of the shoot towards light called?
(ii) What is the downward growth of the roots called?
(iii) Name the hormone responsible for the bending of the shoot.
(iv) Are these movements tropic or nastic?
questions.answer:
(i) PHOTOTROPISM (positive phototropism).
(ii) GEOTROPISM (positive geotropism).
(iii) AUXIN.
(iv) They are TROPIC movements (directional growth responses).
questions.explanation: Phototropism, geotropism, auxin and identifying tropic movement.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In an experiment, the leaves of a Mimosa pudica (touch-me-not) plant folded up immediately when touched. In another plant, tendrils coiled around a stick they came into contact with over a longer time.

(i) What type of movement is the folding of Mimosa leaves?
(ii) What type of tropism is the coiling of tendrils around a support?
(iii) How does the folding of Mimosa leaves differ from the coiling of tendrils in speed and cause?
(iv) What causes the rapid folding of Mimosa leaves?
questions.answer:
(i) A NASTIC movement (non-directional).
(ii) THIGMOTROPISM (response to touch/contact).
(iii) The folding of Mimosa leaves is very fast and is not a growth movement, while the coiling of tendrils is slower and is a directional growth movement (thigmotropism).
(iv) The rapid folding is caused by a sudden change in the water content (turgor) of certain cells at the base of the leaves, not by growth.
questions.explanation: Nastic vs thigmotropic; speed/cause difference; turgor change in Mimosa.
